{{Short description|none}}
This is a glossary of concepts and results in [[real analysis]] and [[complex analysis]] in mathematics. In particular, it includes those in [[measure theory]] (as there is no glossary for measure theory in Wikipedia right now). Also, the topics in [[algebraic analysis]] are included. However, the items in the theory of differential equations are ''not'' included.

See also: [[list of real analysis topics]], [[list of complex analysis topics]] and [[glossary of functional analysis]].

{{compact ToC|side=yes|top=yes|num=yes}}

== 0–9 ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|1=<math>1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots = -\frac{1}{12}</math>}}
{{defn|It means the value of the zeta function at <math>-1</math> is <math>-1/12</math>. See [[1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== A ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Abel}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Abel sum]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Abel integral]]}}

{{term|absolute}}
{{defn|1=A series <math>\sum_0^{\infty} a_n</math> is said to [[absolute convergence|converge absolutely]] if <math>\sum_0^{\infty} |a_n| < \infty.</math>}}

{{term|accumulation}}
{{defn|1=An [[accumulation point]] can mean either a limit point or a cluster point.}}

{{term|analytic capacity}}
{{defn|1=[[analytic capacity]].}}

{{term|analytic continuation}}
{{defn|1=An [[analytic continuation]] of a holomorphic function is a unique holomorphic extension of the function (on a connected open subset of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>).}}

{{term|analytic sheaf}}
{{defn|1=[[analytic sheaf]]}}

{{term|archimedean}}
{{defn|1=The [[archimedean property]] of real numbers says: given two real numbers <math>x, y</math>, if <math>x > 0</math>, then there exists an integer <math>n > 0</math> such that <math>nx > y</math>.}}
{{term|argument principle}}
{{defn|[[argument principle]]}}

{{term|Ascoli}}
{{defn|1=[[Ascoli's theorem]] says that an equicontinous bounded sequence of functions on a compact subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> has a convergent subsequence with respect to the sup norm.}}

{{glossary end}}

== B ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Bargmann}}
{{defn|1=[[Bargmann transform]]}}

{{term|Basel}}
{{defn|1=The [[Basel problem]] says <math>\sum_1^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}.</math>}}

{{term|Berezin}}
{{defn|1=[[Berezin integral]]}}

{{term|Bolzano}}
{{defn|1=The [[Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem]] says a bounded sequence in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> has a convergent subsequence. Today it is subsumed in the statement that a subset of a metric space is compact if and only if it is [[sequentially compact]] (i.e., every sequence has a convergent subsequence) and the [[Heine–Borel theorem]].}}

{{term|Borel}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[Borel measure]] is a measure whose domain is the Borel σ-algebra.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The [[Borel σ-algebra]] on a topological space is the smallest σ-algebra containing all open sets.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Borel's lemma]] says that a given formal power series, there is a smooth function whose Taylor series coincides with the given series.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[Borel–Lebesgue lemma]] is another name for the [[Heine-Borel theorem]].}}

{{term|bounded}}
{{defn|1=A subset <math>A</math> of a metric space <math>(X,d)</math> is [[bounded set|bounded]] if there is some <math>C > 0</math> such that <math>d(a,b) < C</math> for all <math>a,b \in A</math>.}}

{{term|1=bump}}
{{defn|1=A [[bump function]] is a nonzero compactly-supported smooth function, usually constructed using the exponential function.}}

{{term|BV}}
{{defn|1=A [[BV-function]] or a [[bounded variation]] is a function with bounded total variation.}}

{{glossary end}}

== C ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Calderón}}
{{defn|1=[[Calderón–Zygmund lemma]]}}

{{term|Cantor}}
{{defn|1=[[Cantor set]].}}

{{term|capacity}}
{{defn|1=[[Capacity of a set]] is a notion in [[potential theory]].}}

{{term|Carathéodory}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Carathéodory's extension theorem]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Carathéodory's criterion]] states a sufficient condition for Borel sets to be measurable.}}

{{term|Cartan}}
{{defn|1=[[Cartan's theorems A and B]].}}

{{term|Cartwright}}
{{defn|1=[[Cartwright's theorem]] gives a bounded for a ''p''-valent entire function.}}

{{term|Cauchy}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Cauchy–Riemann equations]] are a system of differential equations such that a function satisfying it (in the distribution sense) is a [[holomorphic function]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Cauchy integral formula]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Cauchy residue theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=4|1=[[Cauchy's estimate]].}}
{{defn|no=5|1=The [[Cauchy principal value]] is, when possible, a number assigned to a function when the function is not integrable.}}
{{defn|no=6|1=On a metric space, a sequence <math>x_n</math> is called a [[Cauchy sequence]] if <math>d(x_n, x_m) \to 0</math>; i.e., for each <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there is an <math>N > 0</math> such that <math>d(x_n, x_m) < \epsilon</math> for all <math>n, m \ge N</math>.}}
{{defn|no=7|1=[[Cauchy condensation test]].}}
<!-- well minus doesn’t make sense in general
{{defn|no=7|1=A [[Cauchy net]] is a net <math>x_{\alpha}, \alpha \in I</math> such that the net <math>x_{\alpha} - x_{\beta}, (\alpha, \beta) \in I^2</math> converges to zero, where <math>I^2</math> is preordered pointwise: <math>(\alpha, \beta) \lesssim (\alpha', \beta')</math> if and only if <math>\alpha \lesssim \alpha', \, \beta \lesssim \beta'</math>.}}-->

{{term|Cavalieri}}
{{defn|1=[[Cavalieri's principle]].}}

{{term|Cesàro}}
{{defn|1=[[Cesàro summation]] is one way to compute a [[divergent series]].}}

{{term|Clarke generalized derivative}}
{{defn|1=[[Clarke generalized derivative]].}}

{{term|cluster}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[cluster point]] of a net <math>x_{\alpha}</math> (or a sequence) is a point in <math>\bigcap_{\alpha} \overline{\{ x_{\beta} \mid \beta \gtrsim \alpha \} }</math>. The notion gives a convenient criterion for compactness: a space (resp. a metric space) is compact if and only if each net (resp. sequence) has a cluster point.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=For a [[first countable space]], a point is a cluster point of a sequence <math>x_i</math> if and only if there is a subsequence converging to that point.}}

{{term|complex}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[complex number]] is an element in <math>\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)</math>, the [[quotient ring]] of a polynomial ring, where the image of the indeterminate <math>x</math> is denoted by <math>i</math>. As a set, <math>\mathbb{C}</math> can be identified with <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> and that gives a topology on it.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[complex logarithm]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=Given a function <math>f</math> on an open set <math>U \subset \mathbb{C}</math>, the [[complex derivative]] of it is, if any, the limit <math>\lim_{\mathbb{C} \ni h \to 0} \frac{f(z+h) - f(z)}{h}</math>.}}

{{term|continuous}}
{{defn|1=A function <math>f : X \to Y</math> between metric spaces <math>(X,d_X)</math> and <math>(Y,d_Y)</math> is [[continuous function|continuous]] if for any convergent sequence <math>x_n \to x</math> in <math>X</math>, we have <math>f(x_n) \to f(x)</math> in <math>Y</math>.}}

{{term|contour}}
{{defn|The [[contour integral]] of a measurable function <math>f</math> over a piece-wise smooth curve <math>\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}</math> is <math>\int_{\gamma} f \, dz := \int_0^1 \gamma^*(f \, dz)</math>.}}

{{term|converge}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A sequence <math>x_n</math> in a topological space is said to [[converge (mathematics)|converge]] to a point <math>x</math> if for each open neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>x</math>, the set <math>\{ n \mid x_n \not\in U \}</math> is finite.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A sequence <math>x_n</math> in a metric space is said to converge to a point <math>x</math> if for all <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exists an <math>N > 0</math> such that for all <math>n > N</math>, we have <math>d(x_n,x) < \epsilon</math>.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=A series <math>x_1 + x_2 + \cdots</math> on a normed space (e.g., <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>) is said to [[convergent series|converge]] if the sequence of the partial sums <math>s_n := \sum_1^n x_j</math> converges.}}

{{term|convolution}}
{{defn|1=The [[convolution]] <math>f * g</math> of two functions on a convex set is given by
:<math>(f * g)(x) = \int f(y - x)g(y) \, dy,</math>
provided the integration converges.}}

{{term|Cousin}}
{{defn|1=[[Cousin problems]].}}

{{term|critical}}
{{defn|1=[[critical point]].}}

{{term|cutoff}}
{{defn|1=For sets <math>F \subset U</math>, <math>F</math> closed, <math>U</math> open, a [[cutoff function]] is a function that is <math>1</math> on <math>F</math> and has support contained in <math>U</math>. It’s usually required to be continuous or smooth.}}

{{glossary end}}

== D ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|de Branges}}
{{defn|1=[[de Branges's theorem]].}}

{{term|Dedekind}}
{{defn|A [[Dedekind cut]] is one definition of a real number. By definition, it is a nonempty proper [[lower subset]] <math>\alpha</math> of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> that has no maximal element, where ''lower'' means it contains <math>\{ q \in \mathbb{Q} \mid q < p \}</math> for each <math>p</math> in <math>\alpha</math>. For example, <math>\sqrt{2} = \{ p \in \mathbb{Q} \mid p < 0 \text{ or } p^2 < 2 \}</math>.}}

{{term|derivative}}
{{defn|Given a map <math>f : E \to F</math> between normed spaces, the [[derivative]] of <math>f</math> at a point ''x'' is a (unique) linear map <math>T : E \to F</math> such that <math>\lim_{h \to 0} \| f(x + h) - f(x) - Th \|/\|h\| = 0</math>.}}

{{term|differentiable}}
{{defn|1=A map between normed space is differentiable at a point ''x'' if the derivative at ''x'' exists.}}

{{term|differentiation}}
{{defn|1=[[Differentiation under the integral sign]]}}

{{term|Dini}}
{{defn|1=[[Dini's theorem]].}}

{{term|Dirac}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Dirac delta function]] <math>\delta_0</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is a distribution (so not exactly a function) given as <math>\langle \delta_0, \varphi \rangle = \varphi(0).</math>}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[Dirac sequence]].[https://planetmath.org/diracsequence]}}

{{term|distribution}}
{{defn|1=A [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]] is a type of a generalized function; precisely, it is a continuous linear functional on the space of test functions.}}

{{term|divergent}}
{{defn|1=A [[divergent series]] is a series whose partial sum does not converge. For example, <math>\sum_1^{\infty} \frac{1}{n}</math> is divergent.}}

{{term|division conjecture}}
{{defn|1=The [[division conjecture of L. Schwartz]] (now a theorem) says a distribution divided by a real analytic function is again a distribution.}}

{{term|dominated}}
{{defn|[[Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem]] says <math>\int f_n \, d\mu</math> converges to <math>\int f \, d\mu</math> if <math>f_n</math> is a sequence of measurable functions such that <math>f_n</math> converges to <math>f</math> pointwise and <math>|f_n| \le g</math> for some integrable function <math>g</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

== E ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|e}}
{{defn|[[Euler's number]]. One definition is through the series representation of the exponential function; namely, <math>e = \sum_0^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!}</math>. Another is through natural logarithm; namely, <math>\log(e) = 1</math>.}}

{{term|edge}}
{{defn|[[Edge-of-the-wedge theorem]].}}

{{term|Egoroff}}
{{defn|[[Egoroff's theorem]].}}

{{term|entire}}
{{defn|An [[entire function]] is a holomorphic function whose domain is the entire complex plane.}}

{{term|equicontinuous}}
{{defn|A set <math>S</math> of maps between fixed metric spaces is said to be [[equicontinuous]] if for each <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exists a <math>\delta > 0</math> such that <math>\sup_{f \in S} d(f(x), f(y)) < \epsilon</math> for all <math>x, y</math> with <math>d(x, y) < \delta</math>. A map <math>f</math> is uniformly continuous if and only if <math>\{ f \}</math> is equicontinuous.}}

{{term|1=Euler}}
{{defn|1=The [[Euler–Maclaurin formula]].}}

{{term|1=exponential}}
{{defn|1=The [[exponential function]] is the function <math>z \mapsto e^z</math> on the complex plane, where <math>e</math> is [[Euler's number]]. If the number <math>e</math> is defined through the exponential function, then the exponential function is defined more directly as: <math>z \mapsto \sum_1^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{n!}</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

== F ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Fatou}}
{{defn|[[Fatou's lemma]]}}

{{term|finite interesection property}}
{{defn|Given a topological space <math>X</math>, a family <math>F</math> of closed subsets of <math>X</math> is said to have the [[finite intersection property]] if each finite subset of <math>F</math> has nonempty intersection. Then saying <math>X</math> is compact can be restated as: each family of closed subsets of <math>X</math> with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection.}}

{{term|filter}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[filter (topology)|filter]] <math>F</math> on a set <math>X</math> is a proper subset of the power set of <math>X</math> such that 
:([[upper set|upper]]) if <math>S</math> is in <math>F</math>, each subset of <math>X</math> containing <math>S</math> is also in <math>F</math> and
:([[directed downward|downward directed]]) the intersection of each finite subset of <math>F</math> is in <math>F</math>.
Its role is similar to that of nets but in analysis, nets are more commonly used.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=Given a net <math>x_{\alpha}</math>, there is the filter <math>F</math> determined by it; namely, the filter generated by the tails <math>\{ x_{\beta} \mid \beta \gtrsim \alpha \}</math>. Then for example, <math>x_{\alpha}</math> converges to a point <math>x</math> if and only if <math>F</math> converges to <math>x</math> (meaning <math>F</math> contains every neighborhood of <math>x</math>). Conversely, given a filter, we can choose a net associated to it so that all the associated nets determine the original filter.<ref>{{harvnb|Dugundji|1989|loc=Ch. X., § 2., Remark 1.}}</ref>}}

{{term|first}}
{{defn|1=A [[first countable space]] is a topological space in which each point <math>x</math> has a decreasing sequence of neighborhoods <math>x \in \cdots \subset U_2 \subset U_1 \subset U_0</math> such that each neighborhood of <math>x</math> contains some <math>U_n</math>. An important property of such a space is that a point is in the closure of a set <math>E</math> if and only if there is a sequence in <math>E</math> that converges to that point.}}

{{term|Fock}}
{{defn|[[Fock space]]}}

{{term|Fourier}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Fourier transform]] of a function <math>f</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is: (provided it makes sense)
:<math>\widehat{f}(\xi) = \int f(x) e^{-2\pi i x \cdot \xi} \, dx.</math>}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The Fourier transform <math>\widehat{f}</math> of a distribution <math>f</math> is <math>\langle \widehat{f}, \varphi \rangle = \langle f, \widehat{\varphi} \rangle</math>. For example, <math>\widehat{\delta_0} = 1</math> (Fourier's inversion formula).}}

{{term|Fubini}}
{{defn|[[Fubini's theorem]] computes an integral as iterated integrals.}}

{{glossary end}}

== G ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Gamma}}
{{defn|1=[[Gamma function]].}}

{{term|Gauss}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Gauss–Green formula]]}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Gaussian kernel]]}}

{{term|generalized}}
{{defn|1=A [[generalized function]] is an element of some function space that contains the space of ordinary (e.g., locally integrable) functions. Examples are [[Schwartz's distribution]]s and [[Sato's hyperfunction]]s.}}

{{term|germ}}
{{defn|1=The [[germ of a function]] at a point <math>p</math> is the equivalence class of functions (of some class) on neighborhoods of the point, where <math>f \sim g</math> if the restrictions of <math>f, g</math> are the same on some neighborhood of the point.}}

{{term|Grandi}}
{{defn|1=[[Grandi's series]] is the series <math>\sum_0^{\infty} (-1)^n</math>. It is divergent but some summation methods can be used to show its value is <math>1/2</math>.}}

{{term|Grauert}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Hans Grauert]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Grauert's approximation theorem]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== H ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality}}
{{defn|1=The [[Hardy-Littlewood maximal function]] of <math>f \in L^1(\mathbb R^n)</math> is
:<math>Hf(x) := \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{m(B_r(x))} \int_{B_r(x)} |f|.</math>
The [[Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality]] states that there is some constant <math>C</math> such that for all <math>f \in L^1(\mathbb R^n)</math> and all <math>\alpha > 0</math>,
:<math>m\left(\{ x : Hf(x) > \alpha \}\right) < \frac{C}{\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^n} |f|.</math>}}

{{term|Hardy space}}
{{defn|1=[[Hardy space]]}}

{{term|Hartogs}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Hartogs extension theorem]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Hartogs's theorem on separate holomorphicity]]}}

{{term|harmonic}}
{{defn|1=A function is [[harmonic function|harmonic]] if it satisfies the Laplace equation (in the distribution sense if the function is not twice differentiable).}}

{{term|Hausdorff}}
{{defn|1=The [[Hausdorff–Young inequality]] says that the Fourier transformation <math>\widehat{\cdot} : L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) \to L^{p'}(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> is a well-defined bounded operator when <math>1/p + 1/p' = 1</math>.}} 

{{term|Heaviside}}
{{defn|The [[Heaviside function]] is the function ''H'' on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>H(x) = 1, \, x \ge 0</math> and <math>H(x) = 0, \, x < 0</math>.}}

{{term|Heine}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Heine–Borel theorem]] says a subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The above theorem follows from a more general result: a metric space is compact if and only if it is complete and totally ordered, since a bounded set in a Euclidean space is totally bounded.}}

{{term|Hermite}}
{{defn|1=[[Hermite polynomial]]}}

{{term|Hilbert space}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[Hilbert space]] is a real or complex inner product space that is a complete metric space with the metric induced by the inner product.}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Hilbert transform]].}}

{{term|holomorphic function}}
{{defn|A function defined on an open subset of <math>\mathbb C^n</math> is [[holomorphic]] if it is [[complex differentiable]]. Equivalently, a function is holomorphic if it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations (in the distribution sense if the function is not differentiable).}}

{{term|hypoelliptic}}
{{defn|A [[hypoelliptic operator]] is an operator for which the elliptic regularity holds.}}

{{glossary end}}

== I ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|infinitesimal}}
{{defn|1=An [[infinitesimal]] is a "number" that is greater then zero but is smaller than any positive real number; in particular, it is not a real number.}}

{{term|integrable}}
{{defn|1=A measurable function <math>f</math> is said to be [[integrable function|integrable]] if <math>\int |f| \, d\mu < \infty</math>.}}

{{term|integral}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[integral]] of the [[indicator function]] on a measurable set is the measure (volume) of the set.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=The integral of a measurable function is then defined by approximating the function by linear combinations of indicator functions.}}

{{term|inverse}}
{{defn|1=The [[inverse function theorem]] gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a function to be injective. Note it only gives an "inverse function" on the image of the function.}}

{{term|isolated}}
{{defn|1=An [[isolated point]] of a set is a point that is not a limit point of the set.}}

{{term|isometry}}
{{defn|1=An isometry between metric spaces <math>(X,d_X)</math> and <math>(Y,d_Y)</math> is a bijection <math>f : X \to Y</math> that preserves the metric: <math>d_X(x,x') = d_Y(f(x),f(x'))</math> for all <math>x,x' \in X</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

== J ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|jet}}
{{defn|1=[[jet space]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== L ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Laplace}}
{{defn|1=[[Laplace transform]].}}

{{term|Lebesgue differentiation theorem}}
{{defn|The [[Lebesgue differentiation theorem]] states that for locally integrable <math>f \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)</math>, the equalities
:<math>\lim_{r \to 0} \frac{1}{m(B_r(x))} \int_{B_r(x)} |f(y)-f(x)| \,dy = 0</math>
and
:<math>\lim_{r \to 0} \frac{1}{m(B_r(x))} \int_{B_r(x)} f = f(x)</math>
hold for almost every <math>x</math>. The set where they hold is called the Lebesgue set of <math>f</math>, and points in the Lebesgue set are called [[Lebesgue point]]s.
}}

{{term|Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem}}
{{defn|1=[[Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem]]}}

{{term|Lebesgue}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Lebesgue integral]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Lebesgue measure]].}}
{{defn|no=3|Given an open cover <math>\mathcal{U}</math> of a metric space <math>X</math>, a [[Lebesgue number]] for the cover is a real number <math>\delta > 0</math> such that if <math>S \subset X</math> is a subset of diameter <math>< \delta</math>, then <math>S \subset U</math> for some <math>U \in \mathcal{U}</math>. It exists for example if <math>X</math> is compact.}}

{{term|1=Legendre}}
{{defn|1=[[Legendre transformation]].}}

{{term|Lelong}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Lelong number]].}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[Lelong–Poincaré lemma]].}}

{{term|Levi}}
{{defn|1=[[Levi's problem]] asks to show a pseudoconvex set is a domain of holomorphy.}}

{{term|limit}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[limit of a sequence]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A [[limit point]] <math>p</math> of a subset <math>S</math> of a topological space is a point in the space (not necessarily in <math>S</math>) such that each neighborhood of <math>p</math> intersects <math>S - \{ p \}</math>.}}

{{term|line integral}}
{{defn|A [[line integral]] is an integration over a curve <math>c : I \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>; i.e.,
:<math>\int_c \omega := \int_I c^* \omega.</math>}}

{{term|Liouville}}
{{defn|[[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem]] says a bounded entire function is a constant function.}}

{{term|Lipschitz}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A map <math>f</math> between metric spaces is said to be [[Lipschitz continuous]] if <math>\sup_{x \ne y} \frac{d(f(x), f(y))}{d(x, y)} < \infty</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|A map is locally Lipschitz continuous if it is Lipschitz continuous on each compact subset.}}

{{term|log}}
{{defn|1=The [[natural logarithm]] is the function <math>\log(x) = \int^x_1 \frac{dy}{y}</math>.}}

{{term|Lusin}}
{{defn|[[Lusin's theorem]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== M ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|maximum}}
{{defn|The [[maximum principle]] says that a maximum value of a harmonic function in a connected open set is attained on the boundary.}}

{{term|measurable function}}
{{defn|A [[measurable function]] is a structure-preserving function between measurable spaces in the sense that the preimage of any measurable set is measurable.}}

{{term|measurable set}}
{{defn|A [[measurable set]] is an element of a {{math|σ}}-algebra.}}

{{term|measurable space}}
{{defn|A [[measurable space]] consists of a set and a {{math|σ}}-algebra on that set which specifies what sets are measurable.}}

{{term|measure}}
{{defn|A [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] is a function on a measurable space that assigns to each measurable set a number representing its measure or size. Specifically, if {{math|''X''}} is a set and {{math|''Σ''}} is a {{math|σ}}-algebra on {{math|''X''}}, then a set-function {{math|''μ''}} from {{math|''Σ''}} to the extended real number line is called a measure if the following conditions hold:

*'''Non-negativity''': For all <math>E \in \Sigma, \ \ \mu(E) \geq 0.</math>
*<math>\mu(\varnothing) = 0.</math>
*'''Countable additivity''' (or {{math|''σ''}}-additivity): For all countable collections <math>\{ E_k \}_{k=1}^\infty</math> of pairwise disjoint sets in {{math|''Σ''}},
<math display="block">\mu\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k\right)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \mu(E_k).</math>}}

{{term|measure space}}
{{defn|A [[measure space]] consists of a measurable space and a measure on that measurable space.}}

{{term|meromorphic}}
{{defn|1=A [[meromorphic function]] is an equivalence class of functions that are locally fractions of holomorphic functions.}}

{{term|method of stationary phase}}
{{defn|The [[method of stationary phase]].}}

{{term|metric space}}
{{defn|1=A [[metric space]] is a set {{math|''X''}} equipped with a function <math>d : X \times X \to \mathbb R_{\geq 0}</math>, called a metric, such that (1) <math>d(x,y) = 0</math> iff <math>x=y</math>, (2) <math>d(x,y) \leq d(x,z) + d(z,y)</math> for all <math>x,y,z \in X</math>, (3) <math>d(x,y) = d(y,x)</math> for all <math>x,y \in X</math>.}}

{{term|microfunction}}
{{defn|[[microfunction]]}}

{{term|microlocal}}
{{defn|1=The notion [[microlocal]] refers to a consideration on the cotangent bundle to a space as opposed to that on the space itself. Explicitly, it amounts to considering functions on both points and momenta; not just functions on points.}}

{{term|Minkowski}}
{{defn|1=[[Minkowski inequality]]}}

{{term|modulus}}
{{defn|1=[[modulus of continuity]].}}

{{term|Montel}}
{{defn|1=[[Montel's theorem]].}}

{{term|monotone}}
{{defn|no=1|A sequence of numbers or functions is called monotone or monotonic if it is either weakly increasing <math>x_1 \le x_2 \le \cdots</math> or weakly decreasing.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[monotone convergence theorem for real numbers]] says a monotone sequence is bounded if and only if it converges.}}
{{defn|no=3|[[Lebesgue's monotone convergence theorem]].}}

{{term|Morera}}
{{defn|[[Morera's theorem]] says a function is holomorphic if the integrations of it over arbitrary closed loops are zero.}}

{{term|Morse}}
{{defn|[[Morse function]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== N ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Nash}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Nash function]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Nash–Moser theorem]].}}

{{term|Nevanlinna theory}}
{{defn|1=[[Nevanlinna theory]] concerns meromorphic functions.}}

{{term|1=net}}
{{defn|no=1|1=A [[net (mathematics)|net]] is a generalization of a sequence. Precisely, a ''net'' on a set <math>X</math> is a map from a [[directed set]] to <math>X</math>, where a ''directed set'' is a [[preordered set]] in which each finite subset has an upper bound.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=A net <math>x_{\alpha}</math> ''converges'' to a point <math>x</math> if for each neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>x</math>, there is some <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>\{ x_{\beta} \mid \beta \gtrsim \alpha \} \subset U</math>.}}

{{term|nonmeasurable}}
{{defn|1=Among the consequences of the axiom of choice is that there exists a subset of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> that is not (Lebesgue) measurable, a construction due to Vitali. Note there is a model of set theory in which every subset of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> is measurable so Choice here cannot be avoided.}}

{{term|nonsmooth analysis}}
{{defn|1=[[Nonsmooth analysis]] is a branch of [[mathematical analysis]] that concerns non-smooth functions like Lipschitz functions and has applications to [[optimization theory]] or [[control theory]]. Note this theory is generally different from [[distributional calculus]], a calculus based on distributions.}}

{{term|normed vector space}}
{{defn|A [[normed vector space]], also called a normed space, is a real or complex vector space {{math|''V''}} on which a norm is defined. A norm is a map <math>\lVert\cdot \rVert : V \to \mathbb R</math> satisfying four axioms:

# Non-negativity: for every <math>x\in V</math>,<math>\; \lVert x \rVert \ge 0</math>.
# Positive definiteness: for every <math>x \in V</math>, <math>\; \lVert x\rVert=0</math> if and only if <math>x</math> is the zero vector.
# Absolute homogeneity: for every scalar <math>\lambda</math> and <math>x\in V</math>,<math display="block">\lVert \lambda x \rVert = |\lambda|\, \lVert x\rVert </math>
# Triangle inequality: for every <math>x\in V</math> and <math>y\in V</math>,<math display="block">\|x+y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|.</math>

}}

{{glossary end}}

== O ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Oka}}
{{defn|[[Oka's coherence theorem]] says the sheaf <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^n}</math> of holomorphic functions is [[coherent sheaf|coherent]].}}

{{term|open}}
{{defn|The [[open mapping theorem (complex analysis)]]}}

{{term|oscillatory integral}}
{{defn|1=An [[oscillatory integral]] can give a sense to a formal integral expression like <math>\delta_0(x) = \int e^{2 \pi i x \cdot \xi} \, d\xi.</math>}}

{{glossary end}}

== P ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Paley}}
{{defn|1=[[Paley–Wiener theorem]]}}

{{term|phase}}
{{defn|The [[phase space]] to a configuration space <math>X</math> (in classical mechanics) is the cotangent bundle <math>T^* X</math> to <math>X</math>.}}

{{term|Plancherel}}
{{defn|1=[[Plancherel's theorem]] says the Fourier transformation is a unitary operator.}}

{{term|Plateau}}
{{defn|[[Plateau problem]] concerns the existence of a [[minimal surface]].}}

{{term|plurisubharmonic}}
{{defn|A function <math>f</math> on an open subset <math>U \subset \mathbb{C}</math> is said to be [[plurisubharmonic]] if <math>t \mapsto f(z + tw)</math> is subharmonic for <math>t</math> in a neighborhood of zero in <math>\mathbb{C}</math> and points <math>z, w</math> in <math>U</math>.}}

{{term|Poisson}}
{{defn|1=[[Poisson kernel]]}}

{{term|power series}}
{{defn|A [[power series]] is informally a polynomial of infinite degree; i.e., <math>\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n</math>. (Mathematically, it is the same thing as a sequence <math>a_1, a_2, \cdots, </math> but is usually treated like a polynomial of infinite degree.)}}

{{term|primitive}}
{{defn|1=A [[primitive function]] of a function; another name for an anti-derivative.}}

{{term|pseudoconex}}
{{defn|1=A [[pseudoconvex set]] is a generalization of a convex set.}}

{{term|pseudodifferential}}
{{defn|1=A [[pseudodifferential operator]] is a generalization of a differential operator by allowing symbols to have poles.}}

{{glossary end}}

== R ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Rademacher}}
{{defn|1=[[Rademacher's theorem]] says a locally Lipschitz function is differentiable almost everywhere.}}

{{term|Radon}}
{{defn|no=1|1=Let <math>X</math> be a locally compact Hausdorff space and let <math>I</math> be a positive linear functional on the space of continuous functions with compact support <math>C_c(X)</math>. Positivity means that <math>I(f) \geq 0</math> if <math>f \geq 0</math>. There exist Borel measures <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> such that <math>I(f) = \int f \, d\mu</math> for all <math>f \in C_c(X)</math>. A [[Radon measure]] on <math>X</math> is a Borel measure that is finite on all compact sets, [[outer regular]] on all Borel sets, and [[inner regular]] on all open sets. These conditions guarantee that there exists a ''unique'' Radon measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> such that <math>I(f) = \int f \, d\mu</math> for all <math>f \in C_c(X)</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Radon–Nikodym theorem]].}}

{{term|Ramanujan}}
{{defn|[[Ramanujan summation]].}}

{{term|rank}}
{{defn|1=The [[rank theorem]].}}

{{term|Ray}}
{{defn|1=A [[Ray–Singer metric]].}}

{{term|real}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[real number]] is usually defined as either a [[Dedekind cut]] or an element in the [[Cauchy completion]] of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>. The [[axiom of choice]] is needed to rule out some pathology; for example, without it, there can be an infinite set of real numbers that has no countable subset (which falsifies many basic results).<ref>{{harvnb|Jech|2008|loc=Theorem 10.1.}}</ref>}}
{{defn|no=2|{{quote box|quote=The name "real analysis" is something of an anachronism. Originally applied to the theory of functions of a real variable, it has come to encompass several subjects of a more general and abstract nature that underlie much of modem analysis.|author=G. B. Folland<ref>{{harvnb|Folland|2007|loc=Preface.}}</ref>
|width  = 50% |align  = right}}[[Real analysis]] refers to a study of functions in real variables but may include some functional analysis such as measure theory.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=A [[real-analytic function]] is a function given by a convergent power series.}}

{{term|Riesz}}
{{defn|1=[[Riesz's lemma]] says a closed ball in a normed space is compact if and only if the normed space has finite dimension.}}

{{term|Rellich}}
{{defn|[[Rellich's lemma]] tells when an inclusion of a Sobolev space to another Sobolev space is a compact operator.}}

{{term|residue}}
{{defn|1=See [[Cauchy's residue theorem]].}}

{{term|Riemann}}
{{defn|no=1|The [[Riemann integral]] of a function is either the upper Riemann sum or the lower Riemann sum when the two sums agree.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[Riemann zeta function]] is a (unique) analytic continuation of the function <math>z \mapsto \sum_1^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^z}, \, \operatorname{Re}(z) > 1</math> (it's more traditional to write <math>s</math> for <math>z</math>).}}
{{defn|no=3|The [[Riemann hypothesis]], still a conjecture, says each nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part equal to <math>\frac{1}{2}</math>.}}
{{defn|no=4|[[Riemann's existence theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=5|[[Riemann rearrangement theorem]].}}

{{term|Riesz–Fischer}}
{{defn|The [[Riesz–Fischer theorem]] says the ''L''<sup>''p''</sup> space is complete.}}

{{term|Runge}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Runge's approximation theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Runge domain]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== S ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Sato}}
{{defn|1=[[Sato's hyperfunction]], a type of a generalized function.}}

{{term|Schwarz}}
{{defn|1=A [[Schwarz function]] is a function that is both smooth and rapid-decay.}}

{{term|Schwarz lemma}}
{{defn|1=[[Schwarz lemma]]}}

{{term|semianalytic}}
{{defn|1=The notion of [[semianalytic]] is an analog of semialgebraic.}}

{{term|semicontinuous}}
{{defn|1=A [[semicontinuous function]].}}

{{term|separable}}
{{defn|1=A topological space is [[separable topological space|separable]] if it has a dense at most countable subset.}}

{{term|sequence}}
{{defn|A [[Sequence (mathematics)|sequence]] on a set <math>X</math> is a map <math>\mathbb{N} \to X</math>.}}

{{term|series}}
{{defn|A [[series (mathematics)|series]] is informally an infinite summation process <math>x_1 + x_2 + \cdots</math>. Thus, mathematically, specifying a series is the same as specifying the sequence of the terms in the series. The difference is that, when considering a series, one is often interested in whether the sequence of partial sums <math>s_n := x_1 + \cdots + x_n</math> converges or not and if so, to what.}}

{{term|σ-algebra}}
{{defn|A [[σ-algebra|{{math|σ}}-algebra]] on a set is a nonempty collection of subsets closed under complements, countable unions, and countable intersections.}}

{{term|Stieltjes}}
{{defn|[[Stieltjes–Vitali theorem]]}}

{{term|Stone–Weierstrass theorem}}
{{defn|The [[Stone–Weierstrass theorem]] is any one of a number of related generalizations of the Weierstrass approximation theorem, which states that any continuous real-valued function defined on a closed interval can be uniformly approximated by polynomials. Let <math>X</math> be a compact Hausdorff space and let <math>C(X,\mathbb R)</math> have the uniform metric. One version of the Stone–Weierstrass theorem states that if <math>\mathcal A</math> is a closed subalgebra of <math>C(X,\mathbb R)</math> that separates points and contains a nonzero constant function, then in fact <math>\mathcal A = C(X,\mathbb R)</math>. If a subalgebra is not closed, taking the closure and applying the previous version of the Stone–Weierstrass theorem reveals a different version of the theorem: if <math>\mathcal A</math> is a subalgebra of <math>C(X,\mathbb R)</math> that separates points and contains a nonzero constant function, then <math>\mathcal A</math> is dense in <math>C(X,\mathbb R)</math>.}}

{{term|subanalytic}}
{{defn|1=[[subanalytic]].}}

{{term|subderivative}}
{{defn|1=[[subderivative]].}}

{{term|subharmonic}}
{{defn|1=A twice continuously differentiable function <math>f</math> is said to be [[subharmonic function|subharmonic]] if <math>\Delta f \ge 0</math> where <math>\Delta</math> is the Laplacian. The subharmonicity for a more general function is defined by a limiting process.}}

{{term|subsequence}}
{{defn|1=A [[subsequence]] of a sequence is another sequence contained in the sequence; more precisely, it is a composition <math>\mathbb{N} \overset{j}\to \mathbb{N} \overset{x}\to X</math> where <math>j</math> is a strictly increasing injection and <math>x</math> is the given sequence.}}

{{term|support}}
{{defn|no=1|The [[Support (mathematics)|support of a function]] is the closure of the set of points where the function does not vanish.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[Support (mathematics)#Support of a distribution|support of a distribution]] is the support of it in the sense in sheaf theory.}}

{{term|1=symbol}}
{{defn|1=A symbol is a function on the cotangent bundle (usually required to be continuous or holomorphic or etc.); for example, the [[symbol of a differential operator]].}}

{{term|symmetry}}
{{defn|1=[[symmetry of second derivatives]]. It often holds but not always.}}

{{glossary end}}

== T ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Tauberian}}
{{defn|1=[[Tauberian theory]] is a set of results (called [[tauberian theorem]]s) concerning a divergent series; they are sort of converses to [[abelian theorem]]s but with some additional conditions.}}

{{term|Taylor}}
{{defn|[[Taylor expansion]]}}

{{term|tempered}}
{{defn|A [[tempered distribution]] is a distribution that extends to a continuous linear functional on the space of Schwarz functions.}}

{{term|test}}
{{defn|A [[test function]] is a compactly-supported smooth function; see also [[spaces of test functions and distributions]].}}

{{term|totally bounded}}
{{defn|A metric space is [[totally bounded set|totally bounded]] if, for each <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, it is covered by finitely many open balls of radius <math>\epsilon</math>. A metric space is compact if and only if it is totally bounded and complete.}}

{{glossary end}}

== U ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Ulam}}
{{defn|1=[[Ulam number (measure theory)|Ulam number]]}}

{{term|1=uniform}}
{{defn|no=1|A sequence of maps <math>f_n : X \to E</math> from a topological space to a normed space (e.g., <math>\mathbb R</math>) is said to [[converge uniformly]] to <math>f : X \to E</math> if <math>\operatorname{sup} \| f_n - f \| \to 0</math>.}}
{{defn|no=2|A map between metric spaces is said to be [[uniformly continuous]] if for each <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exist a <math>\delta > 0</math> such that <math>d(f(x), f(y)) < \epsilon</math> for all <math>x, y</math> with <math>d(x, y) < \delta</math>.}}

{{glossary end}}

== V ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|1=Vitali covering lemma}}
{{defn|1=The [[Vitali covering lemma]] states that if <math>\mathcal C</math> is a collection of open balls in <math>\mathbb R^n</math> and
:<math>c < m \left(\bigcup_{B \in \mathcal C} B \right),</math>
then there exists a finite number of balls <math>B_1, \ldots, B_n \in \mathcal C</math> such that
:<math>3^n \sum_{j=1}^n m(B_j) > c.</math>
}}

{{glossary end}}

== W ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|weak}}
{{defn|1=A [[weak solution]] is a generalized function that is a solution of a differential equation.}}

{{term|Weierstrass}}
{{defn|no=1|1=[[Weierstrass preparation theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Weierstrass division theorem]].}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Weierstrass M-test]].}}

{{term|Weitzenböck}}
{{defn|1=[[Weitzenböck formula]].}}

{{term|Weyl}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Weyl calculus]].}}
{{defn|no=2|[[Weyl quantization]].}}

{{term|Whitney}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[Whitney extension theorem]] gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a function to be extended from a closed set to a smooth function on the ambient space.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Whitney topology]]}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Whitney stratification]]}}

{{glossary end}}
